title: Reusable shopping bags
to_item: A folding cotton or canvas tote
why: One sturdy tote does the job of a long run of thin bags that tear, blow away and end up as litter in the desert and the sea.
tip: Keep one folded in the car and one in your daily bag, and hang them by the door as soon as you unpack.
impact_note: Fewer thin bags in circulation means less wind-blown litter and less plastic that animals can swallow.

title: Mesh produce bags
from_item: Thin plastic bags for fruit and vegetables
to_item: Washable mesh produce bags
why: The thin roll bags at the produce counter are used for minutes and are rarely accepted in recycling bins. Mesh bags let the cashier see and weigh what is inside.
tip: Keep the mesh bags inside your tote so they always come shopping with you.
impact_note: Takes one of the hardest plastics to recycle out of your weekly shop.

title: Food wraps
to_item: Beeswax wraps, or a plate over the bowl
why: Cling film is thin, often greasy after use and almost never recycled. Wax wraps are washed and reused for months, and a plate on a bowl costs nothing.
tip: Warm the wrap in your hands so it grips the rim, and wash it in cool soapy water because heat melts the wax.
impact_note: Replaces a daily kitchen plastic that nearly always ends up in general waste.

title: Bring your own container
to_item: Your own lunch box or steel tiffin
why: Takeaway tubs are usually stained with oil and sauce, which keeps them out of recycling. Many restaurants will happily fill a clean container you bring.
tip: Ask at the counter when you order in person, and tick the no-cutlery option in delivery apps.
impact_note: Each refill of your own box replaces a tub that would most likely go to landfill.

title: Refillable coffee capsules
to_item: A refillable steel capsule, or a French press
why: Capsules mix plastic or aluminium with wet coffee grounds, so few of them are ever recycled. A refillable capsule works in the same machine with any ground coffee.
tip: Buy a fine espresso grind, press it down lightly, and rinse the capsule straight after brewing.
impact_note: Your daily coffee leaves only the coffee bag and compostable grounds behind.

title: Refillable water
to_item: A dispenser with returnable large bottles, or a filter jug
why: Small water bottles are the biggest source of plastic bottles in many homes. Large dispenser bottles are collected, cleaned and refilled by the supplier, and a filter jug needs no bottles at all.
tip: Ask your water supplier for returnable bottles, and fill a steel bottle from the dispenser before you leave home.
impact_note: Replaces a steady stream of small bottles with containers that are used again and again.

title: Your own bottle on the go
from_item: Chilled drinks bought in plastic bottles
to_item: An insulated steel bottle
why: An insulated bottle keeps water cold for hours in the heat, so you stop buying chilled drinks in plastic on the way.
tip: Fill it with ice and water in the morning, and look for refill fountains in parks, malls and offices.
impact_note: Every refill is one less bottle to collect, sort and recycle.

title: Reusable straws
to_item: A steel or glass straw, or no straw
why: Straws are too small and light to be sorted at recycling plants, so they end up as litter or landfill. Most drinks do not need one at all.
tip: Say no straw when you order, and keep a steel straw with its little brush in your bag if you like one.
impact_note: Small plastics like straws are among the most common finds on beaches.

title: Washable kitchen cloths
to_item: Washable cotton cloths and old t-shirt rags
why: Kitchen roll cannot be recycled once it is greasy or wet. Cloths wipe better and simply go in the wash with the towels.
tip: Cut an old t-shirt into squares, keep them in a jar by the sink, and drop used ones in a small basket until laundry day.
impact_note: Saves paper that is used for seconds, and gives worn clothes a second job.

title: Washable wipes
to_item: A damp washcloth or washable cotton wipes
why: Most wet wipes contain plastic fibres that do not break down, and they block drains when flushed.
tip: Keep a small stack of cotton wipes and a spray bottle of water by the sink or changing mat.
impact_note: Keeps plastic fibres out of drains, sewers and the sea.

title: Safety razor
title_ar: ماكينة حلاقة معدنية بشفرات قابلة للاستبدال
to_item: A metal safety razor with replaceable blades
why: A disposable razor throws away a whole plastic handle because the blade went dull. A safety razor keeps its handle for years and only the thin steel blade changes.
tip: Shave with light pressure and a shallow angle, and collect used blades in a closed tin before handing it in as scrap metal.
impact_note: Mixed plastic and metal waste becomes a small amount of clean steel.

title: Plant-based dish scrubbers
to_item: A loofah, cellulose sponge or wooden dish brush
why: Foam sponges shed tiny plastic bits with every wash and wear out fast. Loofah and cellulose scrubbers can be composted when they are done.
tip: Let the scrubber dry on a rack between uses so it lasts longer and stays fresh.
impact_note: Fewer microplastics washed down the sink.

title: Bamboo toothbrush
to_item: A bamboo toothbrush, or an electric brush with replaceable heads
why: Toothbrushes are replaced often and are not taken by household recycling. A bamboo handle is plant-based, so only the small bristle tuft is plastic.
tip: Pull the bristles out with pliers before composting the handle, or reuse the handle as a plant marker.
impact_note: Swaps a solid plastic handle for a plant-based one.

title: Loose-leaf tea
to_item: Loose-leaf tea with a steel strainer or teapot
why: Many tea bags are sealed with a plastic that does not break down in compost. Loose tea needs no bag at all, and the used leaves compost completely.
tip: Brew in a strainer or small teapot, then tip the used leaves onto your plants or into the compost.
impact_note: The used leaves become clean compost instead of mixed waste.

title: Reusable food bags
to_item: Silicone bags or glass containers with lids
why: Zip bags are hard to clean and usually thrown away after one use. Silicone bags and glass boxes handle the freezer, the dishwasher and years of use.
tip: Label a few clean glass jars for the freezer and leave space at the top so they do not crack.
impact_note: One small set replaces box after box of zip bags.

title: Lids instead of foil
to_item: Dishes with lids, or silicone stretch lids
why: Foil is only recyclable when it is clean and scrunched into a ball, so food-covered foil usually ends up in the bin. A lid does the same job every day.
tip: Cover oven dishes with an oven-safe lid or an upturned baking tray, and save foil for the jobs only foil can do.
impact_note: Less aluminium, a metal that takes a lot of energy to make, used just once.

title: Silicone baking mat
to_item: A silicone baking mat, or a lightly greased tray
why: Baking paper is coated so food does not stick, which also stops it being recycled with paper. A mat is wiped clean and reused for years.
tip: Choose a mat that fits your most used tray and store it flat or loosely rolled.
impact_note: Removes a coated paper that can only go to landfill.

title: Rechargeable batteries
to_item: Rechargeable NiMH batteries and a charger
why: Single-use batteries are hazardous waste that has to go to a collection point. Rechargeables are refilled hundreds of times, so far fewer batteries need safe disposal.
tip: Start with the devices that eat batteries fastest, like remotes and game controllers, and keep a charged spare set in a drawer.
impact_note: Far fewer batteries to collect and treat as hazardous waste.

title: Reusable cup
to_item: A reusable cup with a lid
why: Paper cups are lined with plastic to hold liquid, so most cannot be recycled with paper. Many cafes are glad to fill your own cup.
tip: Rinse it right after use and keep it on your desk or in the car so it is there for the next coffee.
impact_note: Replaces lined cups and plastic lids that usually end up in general waste.

title: Travel cutlery set
to_item: A travel set of metal or bamboo cutlery
why: Plastic forks and spoons are used for a few minutes and are too small for recycling plants to sort. A travel set fits in a bag or a desk drawer.
tip: Choose no cutlery in delivery apps and keep a set in your work bag.
impact_note: Removes small plastics that recycling plants cannot sort.

title: Detergent refills
from_item: A new detergent bottle every time
to_item: Refill pouches, concentrates or a refill station
why: A refill pouch or a concentrate uses much less plastic than a new rigid bottle, and the bottle you already own lasts for years.
tip: Keep your sturdiest bottle, label it, and buy the largest refill or concentrate you have room to store.
impact_note: Less rigid plastic for every load of washing.

title: Shampoo bars
to_item: A shampoo bar
why: A shampoo bar is shampoo without the water and without the bottle. It usually comes in a paper box and lasts as long as a bottle or longer.
tip: Rub the bar between wet hands rather than on your hair, and keep it on a draining dish so it dries between washes.
impact_note: No bottle and no pump, only a paper box that recycles.

title: Bar soap
from_item: Liquid hand soap in pump bottles
to_item: A bar of soap on a draining dish
why: Pump bottles combine several plastics and a metal spring that recycling plants cannot separate. A bar of soap has almost no packaging.
tip: A slatted soap dish keeps the bar dry so it lasts and does not go soft.
impact_note: Removes one of the hardest bathroom items to recycle.

title: Fabric gift wrap
to_item: A fabric wrap, a scarf or reused paper
why: Glossy, glittery or metallic wrapping paper cannot be recycled, and it is torn off within seconds. A fabric wrap becomes part of the gift.
tip: Place the box in the middle of the fabric and tie opposite corners in a knot on top; no tape needed.
impact_note: Keeps coated paper and tape out of the bin at every celebration.

title: Buy less, buy second-hand
to_item: Second-hand finds, clothes swaps and fewer well-made pieces
why: Cheap clothes are often worn a few times and then thrown away. Second-hand and well-made pieces stay in use far longer.
tip: Before buying, ask yourself whether you will wear it many times, and try a swap with friends or a thrift shop first.
impact_note: Keeping a garment in use for longer is one of the most effective ways to cut its footprint.

title: Print less
to_item: Double-sided printing, recycled paper or reading on screen
why: Double-sided printing uses half the sheets for the same pages, and a lot of printing is not needed at all.
tip: Make double-sided the default in your printer settings and keep a tray of misprints for notes.
impact_note: Less paper bought, and the paper you do use is easy to recycle.

title: Cloth napkins
to_item: Cloth napkins
why: Used napkins are too dirty to recycle. Cloth napkins go in the wash with the rest of the laundry and look nicer on the table.
tip: Give everyone their own napkin ring or clip so a napkin can be used for more than one meal.
impact_note: Removes a daily single-use paper from the table.

title: Reusable plates for gatherings
from_item: Disposable plates and cups for gatherings
to_item: A shared set of reusable or borrowed tableware
why: Party plates are greasy and made of mixed materials, so they leave by the bin bag. A set of sturdy reusable plates serves every gathering.
tip: Keep a box of melamine or enamel plates for guests, and lend it to neighbours for their gatherings.
impact_note: The plates fill the dishwasher instead of the bin.

title: Fewer flyers and receipts
to_item: A no-flyers sign and digital receipts
why: Flyers go straight from the door to the bin, and shiny thermal receipts should not go in paper recycling.
tip: Put a small no-flyers sign on your door and choose e-receipts at the checkout.
impact_note: Stops paper waste before it reaches your home.

title: Paper-stem or reusable cotton buds
title_ar: أعواد قطن بساق ورقية أو قابلة لإعادة الاستخدام
to_item: Paper-stem buds or a washable silicone swab
why: Plastic stems are small, light and often flushed, so they are a common sight on beaches. Paper stems compost, and silicone swabs are washed and reused.
tip: Keep them in a lidded jar next to a small bin, never next to the toilet.
impact_note: Keeps a small, often flushed plastic out of the sea.

title: Reusable period products
title_ar: منتجات دورة شهرية قابلة لإعادة الاستخدام
to_item: A menstrual cup, period underwear or washable pads
why: Disposable pads contain plastic layers and are thrown away every cycle. Reusable options last for years with good care.
tip: Try one reusable product alongside your usual ones first, and follow the maker's cleaning instructions.
impact_note: Replaces a regular stream of plastic-lined waste.

title: Cloth nappies
to_item: Modern cloth nappies, even part-time
why: Disposable nappies are one of the bulkiest things in a family's bin, and they cannot be recycled. Cloth nappies are washed and reused through the baby years.
tip: Start part-time at home, and give them a cold rinse before a warm wash.
impact_note: Even part-time use takes a large share of volume out of the bin.

title: Reuse glass jars for storage
to_item: Clean glass jars from your own kitchen
why: Jam, sauce and honey jars are free, clear and airtight, and glass does not stain or hold smells the way old plastic tubs do.
tip: Soak jars in warm soapy water to lift the labels, and keep each lid with its jar.
impact_note: Gives jars a long second life before they go to the glass bank.

title: Bulk snacks in a lunch box
title_ar: وجبات خفيفة بالجملة في علبة طعام
to_item: Larger packs portioned into a lunch box
why: Small snack packets are usually metallised plastic that no household bin can recycle. One large pack means far less packaging per portion.
tip: Portion snacks into small reusable boxes at the weekend so school and work mornings stay quick.
impact_note: Fewer multi-layer wrappers, which household recycling cannot take.

title: Skip the aerosol air freshener
to_item: Fresh air, a reed diffuser or an open jar of baking soda
why: Aerosol cans are pressurised and must be handled as hazardous waste unless completely empty. Airing rooms in the cooler hours, a reed diffuser or baking soda deal with most smells.
tip: Leave an open jar of baking soda in the fridge or wardrobe and replace it every few months.
impact_note: One less pressurised can to dispose of safely.

title: LED bulbs
to_item: LED bulbs
why: LED bulbs last many times longer and use much less electricity. Fluorescent bulbs contain mercury and need hazardous waste collection when they fail.
tip: Replace bulbs as they burn out, starting with the lights you use most, and take old fluorescent ones to a collection point.
impact_note: Fewer bulbs to replace, and no mercury in the new ones.

title: Refillable cleaning spray
from_item: A new spray cleaner bottle every time
to_item: One refillable spray bottle with a concentrate
why: A trigger spray bottle outlasts many refills. Concentrates are mostly water you add at home, so less plastic and less weight is shipped.
tip: Label the bottle with what is inside, and never mix vinegar or ammonia cleaners with bleach.
impact_note: One trigger bottle instead of a new one with every purchase.

title: Repair or buy refurbished
title_ar: أصلح جهازك أو اشترِ جهازًا مجدّدًا
to_item: Repairing, replacing the battery, or buying refurbished
why: Most of a device's footprint comes from making it, so every extra year of use matters more than recycling it at the end.
tip: Back up your data, then ask a reputable repair shop about a new battery or screen before you replace the whole device.
impact_note: Keeping a device longer delays e-waste and avoids making a new one.

title: Refillable pens
to_item: A refillable pen
why: Disposable pens are thrown away with almost all their plastic intact. A refillable pen only needs a new ink cartridge.
tip: Buy a few refills together with the pen so you are never tempted to grab a disposable one.
impact_note: A small daily plastic that adds up across a school or an office.

title: Fewer bin liners
from_item: A new plastic liner in every small bin
to_item: Unlined small bins emptied into one main bag
why: Small bins that collect dry waste do not need their own liner. Emptying them into one kitchen bag cuts the number of bags you use.
tip: Line only the kitchen bin, and wipe or rinse the small bins now and then.
impact_note: Fewer plastic bags used only to carry waste away.

title: Read the news on screen
from_item: Printed newspapers and magazines you only skim
to_item: Digital editions, or copies at the library
why: Papers you skim once pile up fast. Digital editions often cost less, and a library shares one printed copy among many readers.
tip: Switch the subscription you read least first, and keep old papers clean and dry for recycling.
impact_note: Less paper printed, delivered and collected.

title: Compost food scraps
from_item: Food scraps in the general bin
to_item: A small compost bin or bokashi bucket
why: Food scraps make the general bin wet and smelly and spoil anything that could have been recycled. Composted, they feed plants instead.
tip: Keep a lidded caddy by the sink for peels and grounds, and add dry leaves or shredded cardboard to the compost to balance it.
impact_note: Turns the wettest part of household waste into soil for your plants.
